title: Descriptive Statistics
description: Mean vs median under skew, n − 1 variance, IQR and the 1.5×IQR outlier rule, z-scores, the 68-95-99.7 rule, and linear transformations.

cards.title: What is the median of 3, 8, 1, 10, 6, 4?
cards.body:
5

Sort first: $1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10$. With an even count, the **median** is the mean of the two middle values: $\frac{4 + 6}{2} = 5$.

Watch out: skipping the sort would average the unsorted middle pair, 1 and 10, and give $5.5$.
cards.searchQuery: median of even number of values

cards.title: In a strongly right-skewed distribution, which is usually larger: the mean or the median?
cards.body:
The mean

A few very large values in the right tail pull the **mean** up, while the median stays with the bulk of the data.

Example: incomes are the classic right-skewed case.
Tip: left skew usually puts the mean below the median; for symmetric data the two are about equal.
cards.searchQuery: right skewed mean greater than median

cards.title: Which common summary statistics are resistant to outliers, and which are not?
cards.body:
Resistant: **median** and **IQR**. Not resistant: mean, standard deviation, range.

One extreme value drags the mean and inflates the SD and range, but barely moves the middle of the sorted data.

Tip: for skewed data or data with outliers, report the median and IQR.

cards.title: What is the five-number summary, and which plot is built from it?
cards.body:
Minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum

A **boxplot** draws a box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ with a line at the median. In the usual (modified) boxplot, the whiskers reach the most extreme points within the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ fences, and points beyond them are plotted individually as outliers.

Key idea: the five numbers split the sorted data into four parts of about 25% each.

cards.title: A data set has $Q_1 = 20$ and $Q_3 = 35$. Above what value is a point flagged as an outlier by the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule?
cards.body:
57.5

$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 15$, so the fences are $Q_1 - 1.5(15) = -2.5$ and $Q_3 + 1.5(15) = 35 + 22.5 = 57.5$.

Watch out: points beyond a fence are only flagged as **potential outliers**. The rule is a rule of thumb, not proof.

cards.title: In the sample variance $s^2$, what is the sum of squared deviations divided by?
cards.body:
$n - 1$

$s^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$

Why: the deviations from $\bar{x}$ always sum to 0, so only $n - 1$ of them are free (the **degrees of freedom**). Dividing by $n$ would systematically underestimate $\sigma^2$.

cards.title: What is the sample standard deviation of the data 1, 3, 5?
cards.body:
2

$\bar{x} = 3$. The squared deviations $4, 0, 4$ sum to $8$, so $s^2 = \frac{8}{3 - 1} = 4$ and $s = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

Watch out: dividing by $n$ instead would give $\sqrt{8/3} \approx 1.63$, the wrong answer for a sample.

cards.title: Lengths are measured in cm. Why is the standard deviation easier to interpret than the variance?
cards.body:
The SD is in $\mathrm{cm}$, the same units as the data; the variance is in $\mathrm{cm}^2$.

Variance averages **squared** deviations, so its units are squared. Taking the square root returns to the original scale.

Key idea: the SD reads as a typical distance from the mean.

cards.title: Maya scored 85 on a test with mean 75, SD 5. Leo scored 90 on a test with mean 80, SD 10. Who did better relative to their class?
cards.body:
Maya

Standardizing with $z = \frac{x - \text{mean}}{\text{SD}}$ puts both scores on one scale. Maya: $z = \frac{85 - 75}{5} = 2.0$. Leo: $z = \frac{90 - 80}{10} = 1.0$.

Key idea: Maya is 2 SDs above her class mean, Leo only 1. Raw points can't be compared across different tests.

cards.title: Scores have mean 70 and SD 8. What score has a z-score of $-1.5$?
cards.body:
58

Solve $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ for $x$: $x = \mu + z\sigma = 70 + (-1.5)(8) = 70 - 12 = 58$.

Tip: a negative **z-score** means the value is below the mean.

cards.title: After converting every value in a data set to a z-score, what are the new mean and standard deviation?
cards.body:
Mean $0$, SD $1$

Subtracting the mean shifts the center to 0, and dividing by the SD rescales the spread to 1.

Watch out: the shape doesn't change. Z-scores of skewed data are still skewed, not normal.

cards.title: What does the empirical rule say, and what kind of data does it apply to?
cards.body:
About $68\%$, $95\%$ and $99.7\%$ of values lie within $1$, $2$ and $3$ SD of the mean.

In symbols: $\mu \pm \sigma$, $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ and $\mu \pm 3\sigma$.

Watch out: it applies only to roughly **normal** (unimodal, symmetric, bell-shaped) data. For skewed data these percentages can be far off.

cards.title: Heights are roughly normal with mean $170\,\mathrm{cm}$ and SD $10\,\mathrm{cm}$. By the empirical rule, about what percent are taller than $190\,\mathrm{cm}$?
cards.body:
About $2.5\%$

$190 = 170 + 2(10)$ is 2 SD above the mean. About 95% of values lie within 2 SD, leaving 5% in the two tails.

Why: by symmetry, half of that 5% is above $190\,\mathrm{cm}$.

cards.title: Daily highs have mean $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and SD $5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. After converting with $F = 1.8C + 32$, what is the SD in $^\circ\mathrm{F}$?
cards.body:
$9\,^\circ\mathrm{F}$

For $y = a + bx$, the mean becomes $a + b\bar{x}$ but the SD becomes $|b|\,s$. So the SD is $1.8 \times 5 = 9$.

Watch out: adding 32 shifts the center, not the spread. (The mean becomes $1.8(20) + 32 = 68\,^\circ\mathrm{F}$.)
cards.searchQuery: SD after linear transformation Celsius Fahrenheit

cards.title: What is the difference between descriptive and inferential statistics?
cards.body:
Descriptive statistics **summarize the data in hand**; inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population.

Descriptive tools are graphs and numbers such as the mean and SD. Inferential methods add a measure of uncertainty.

Example: "the 200 students surveyed have a mean GPA of 3.1" is descriptive. "We're 95% confident the mean GPA of all students here is between 3.0 and 3.2" is inferential.

cards.title: In statistics, what is the difference between a population and a sample?
cards.body:
The **population** is the entire group a study wants to describe; a **sample** is the part of it actually observed.

Example: all 30,000 students at a university (population) vs. the 400 who answer a survey (sample).

Watch out: conclusions extend to the population only if the sample represents it, ideally through random selection.

cards.title: What is a census, and why do studies usually sample instead?
cards.body:
A census collects data from **every member** of the population.

Censuses are expensive and slow, and sometimes impossible. A well-chosen sample estimates population values at a fraction of the cost.

Example: testing every light bulb until it burns out would leave none to sell.

cards.title: Is the mean GPA of a random sample of 50 students a parameter or a statistic?
cards.body:
A statistic

A **statistic** describes a sample and changes from sample to sample. A **parameter** describes the whole population and is usually unknown.

Mnemonic: Sample goes with Statistic, Population with Parameter.

cards.title: Which symbols denote the population mean and SD, and which denote the sample mean and SD?
cards.body:
Population: $\mu$ and $\sigma$. Sample: $\bar{x}$ and $s$.

Greek letters usually mark **parameters** and Latin letters mark **statistics**.

Tip: likewise, $p$ is a population proportion and $\hat{p}$ is a sample proportion.
cards.searchQuery: population and sample notation mu sigma x-bar s

cards.title: What distinguishes a categorical variable from a quantitative one?
cards.body:
A **categorical** variable places each individual in a group; a **quantitative** variable takes numerical values for which arithmetic makes sense.

Example: blood type and major are categorical; height and income are quantitative.

Tip: would an average of the values mean anything? If not, the variable is categorical.

cards.title: ZIP codes are written with digits. Is ZIP code a categorical or a quantitative variable?
cards.body:
Categorical

ZIP codes are labels for places; their average or difference means nothing.

Watch out: being written with digits doesn't make a variable quantitative. Jersey numbers and phone numbers are the same.

cards.title: Is the number of siblings a person has a discrete or a continuous variable?
cards.body:
Discrete

It takes separate, countable values ($0, 1, 2, \dots$) with nothing in between.

Key idea: a **continuous** variable, such as height or time, can take any value in an interval, limited only by how precisely it's measured.
cards.searchQuery: discrete vs continuous variable number of siblings

cards.title: What are the four levels of measurement, from least to most informative?
cards.body:
Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio

- **Nominal**: names only (blood type)
- **Ordinal**: ordered, but gaps aren't equal (letter grades)
- **Interval**: equal gaps, no true zero (Celsius temperature)
- **Ratio**: equal gaps and a true zero (mass, elapsed time)

Mnemonic: NOIR.

cards.title: Survey responses range from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. At which level of measurement are they?
cards.body:
Ordinal

The categories have a natural order, but the steps between them aren't known to be equal. Is "neutral" to "agree" the same distance as "agree" to "strongly agree"?

Watch out: differences and averages of the numeric codes are therefore questionable.
cards.searchQuery: ordinal level of measurement Likert scale

cards.title: Which level of measurement has a true zero, so that statements like 'twice as much' make sense?
cards.body:
Ratio

Zero means **none of the quantity** ($0\,\mathrm{kg}$, $0\,\mathrm{s}$, $0\,\mathrm{K}$), so $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ really is twice $20\,\mathrm{kg}$.

Watch out: interval scales such as Fahrenheit temperature have equal steps but an arbitrary zero.

cards.title: Why is it wrong to say that $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is twice as hot as $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
cards.body:
Celsius is an **interval** scale: its zero is a convention, not an absence of heat, so ratios of Celsius values are meaningless.

Example: on the kelvin scale, which has a true zero, $293.15\,\mathrm{K}$ is only about 3.5% more than $283.15\,\mathrm{K}$.

Tip: differences are fine. $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

cards.title: Which graphs display the distribution of a single categorical variable?
cards.body:
**Bar charts** and **pie charts**

Bars show each category's count or percent. A pie chart shows parts of one whole, so its categories must cover 100% of the group.

Watch out: histograms, dotplots and boxplots are for quantitative data.
cards.searchQuery: graphs for categorical data bar chart pie chart

cards.title: Why compare two groups of different sizes with relative frequencies (percents) rather than counts?
cards.body:
Counts grow with group size; **percents** put both groups on the same scale.

Example: 30 smokers out of 100 vs. 45 out of 300. The second group has more smokers but a lower rate ($15\%$ vs. $30\%$).
cards.searchQuery: relative frequency vs counts comparing groups

cards.title: How does a histogram differ from a bar chart?
cards.body:
A **histogram** shows a quantitative variable: its bars cover adjacent numeric intervals, so they touch and their order is fixed. A **bar chart** shows a categorical variable: its bars are separate and can be listed in any order.

Key idea: shape (skew, modes) is meaningful for a histogram, not for a bar chart of unordered categories.

cards.title: How can the choice of bin width change what a histogram shows?
cards.body:
Very wide bins hide detail, even a second peak; very narrow bins make the shape jagged and noisy.

The data don't change, only the picture.

Tip: try a few **bin widths** before describing a distribution's shape.
cards.searchQuery: histogram bin width effect on shape

cards.title: What does a stemplot (stem-and-leaf plot) show that a histogram does not?
cards.body:
The individual data values

Each value splits into a **stem** (leading digits) and a **leaf** (last digit): 47 is stem 4, leaf 7. You see the shape like a sideways histogram and can still read off every value, for example to find the median.

Watch out: stemplots work best for small data sets.

cards.title: Which graph best shows how one quantitative variable changes over time?
cards.body:
A **time plot** (time series plot)

Time goes on the horizontal axis, the variable on the vertical axis, with points connected in time order.

Why: it reveals trends, seasonal cycles and sudden shifts that a histogram of the same values would hide.

cards.title: A histogram has a long tail stretching toward large values. What is its shape called?
cards.body:
Skewed right (positively skewed)

Skew is named for the direction of the **long tail**, not the peak. Here the peak sits on the left.

Example: incomes, house prices and waiting times are typically skewed right.

cards.title: On an easy exam, most scores fall between 90 and 100 and a few are much lower. What shape is the distribution?
cards.body:
Skewed left

Scores pile up against the 100-point ceiling and trail off toward low values, so the long tail points left.

Tip: expect the mean to fall below the median.
cards.searchQuery: left skewed distribution easy exam scores

cards.title: A histogram shows two distinct peaks. What does this bimodal shape usually suggest?
cards.body:
The data may combine two different groups or processes.

Example: Old Faithful's waiting times between eruptions cluster around a short and a long value.

Watch out: a single mean or median of a **bimodal** distribution can describe almost nobody. Look for the variable that separates the groups.

cards.title: When describing the distribution of a quantitative variable, what four features should you cover?
cards.body:
Shape, center, spread and unusual features (outliers, gaps, clusters), all in context.

Example: "Commute times are skewed right, with median $22\,\mathrm{min}$ and IQR $15\,\mathrm{min}$; one commute of $95\,\mathrm{min}$ is a high outlier."

Mnemonic: **SOCS**: shape, outliers, center, spread.
cards.searchQuery: describe distribution shape center spread outliers

cards.title: In a density histogram, a bin of width 5 holds 20% of the data. How tall is its bar?
cards.body:
0.04 (per unit of the variable)

Height $= \dfrac{\text{relative frequency}}{\text{bin width}} = \dfrac{0.20}{5} = 0.04$.

Why: each bar's **area** then equals its share of the data, and the areas sum to 1.
Tip: use this scale whenever bins have unequal widths.
cards.searchQuery: density histogram bar height relative frequency bin width

cards.title: A cumulative relative frequency table shows 35% of values at most 20 and 80% at most 30. What fraction of values are above 20 but at most 30?
cards.body:
0.45

Subtract the cumulative values: $0.80 - 0.35 = 0.45$, i.e. 45% of the data.

Key idea: cumulative frequencies never decrease and end at 1 (100%); their graph is called an **ogive**.

cards.title: What is the formula for the sample mean $\bar{x}$ of $n$ values $x_1, \dots, x_n$?
cards.body:
$\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}$

Add the values and divide by how many there are.

Tip: the population mean $\mu$ is the same calculation over all $N$ values of the population.

cards.title: A sorted data set has $n = 25$ values. In which position is the median?
cards.body:
The 13th

For odd $n$, the median is the value in position $\frac{n + 1}{2} = \frac{26}{2} = 13$, with 12 values on each side.

Tip: for even $n$, average the values in positions $\frac{n}{2}$ and $\frac{n}{2} + 1$.

cards.title: Which measure of center is the only one that makes sense for nominal data such as favorite color?
cards.body:
The **mode**, the most frequent value

Colors can't be averaged or put in order, so the mean and median don't exist. You can still say which category is most common.
cards.searchQuery: mode nominal data measure of center

cards.title: Which measures of center are appropriate for ordinal data such as letter grades?
cards.body:
The median and the mode

Ordinal values can be sorted, so a middle value exists. But the gaps between categories aren't equal, so a mean of the codes isn't meaningful.

Watch out: nominal data allow only the **mode**.
cards.searchQuery: measure of center ordinal data median mode

cards.title: What is the mode of the data 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 9?
cards.body:
3 and 7: the data are **bimodal**.

Both values appear twice, more often than any other.

Tip: a data set can have one mode, several, or none at all (when every value appears equally often).

cards.title: Exams count 60% and homework 40% of a course grade. A student averages 80 on exams and 90 on homework. What is the course grade?
cards.body:
84

A **weighted mean** multiplies each value by its weight: $\bar{x}_w = \dfrac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i} = 0.6(80) + 0.4(90) = 48 + 36 = 84$.

Watch out: the plain average of 80 and 90 ($85$) ignores that exams count more.

cards.title: The values 1, 2 and 3 occur with frequencies 2, 5 and 3. What is the mean?
cards.body:
2.1

$\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i} = \dfrac{1(2) + 2(5) + 3(3)}{2 + 5 + 3} = \dfrac{21}{10} = 2.1$

Watch out: averaging just the distinct values $1, 2, 3$ gives $2$ and ignores how often each occurs.

cards.title: The values 10, 20, 30 and 40 occur with frequencies 3, 4, 2 and 1. What is the median?
cards.body:
20

There are $n = 10$ values, so the median averages the 5th and 6th in order. Positions 1 to 3 hold 10 and positions 4 to 7 hold 20, so both middle values are 20.

Watch out: the median of the four distinct values ($25$) ignores the frequencies.

cards.title: Grouped data: 5 values in $[0, 10)$, 10 in $[10, 20)$ and 5 in $[20, 30)$. Using class midpoints, what is the estimated mean?
cards.body:
15

Treat every value as its **class midpoint** ($5$, $15$, $25$): $\dfrac{5(5) + 10(15) + 5(25)}{20} = \dfrac{300}{20} = 15$.

Watch out: it's only an estimate, because the exact values within each class are unknown.
cards.searchQuery: estimate mean grouped data class midpoints

cards.title: A variable is coded 1 for 'yes' and 0 for 'no'. In a sample of 50, 18 answered yes. What is the mean of the variable?
cards.body:
0.36

$\bar{x} = \dfrac{18(1) + 32(0)}{50} = 0.36$

Key idea: the mean of a 0/1 variable is the **proportion** of 1s, $\hat{p}$. That's why sample proportions behave like sample means in many formulas.

cards.title: Section A has 10 students with mean score 70; section B has 30 students with mean 80. What is the mean of all 40 students?
cards.body:
77.5

Combine the totals: $\dfrac{10(70) + 30(80)}{40} = \dfrac{700 + 2400}{40} = 77.5$.

Watch out: averaging the two means ($75$) is wrong unless the groups are the same size. The larger group pulls the result toward its mean.
cards.searchQuery: combined mean of two groups weighted

cards.title: A student's first four test scores average 85. What score on the fifth test makes the five-test average 87?
cards.body:
95

Work with **totals**: five tests averaging 87 need $5 \times 87 = 435$ points, and the first four contribute $4 \times 85 = 340$.

So the fifth must be $435 - 340 = 95$.
cards.searchQuery: score needed to reach target average

cards.title: For any data set, what does $\sum (x_i - \bar{x})$ equal?
cards.body:
0

The mean is the balance point: positive and negative deviations cancel exactly, since $\sum x_i - n\bar{x} = 0$.

Why: that's why measures of spread **square** the deviations (or take absolute values) before averaging.
cards.searchQuery: sum of deviations from the mean equals zero

cards.title: The data 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 have mean 4 and median 4. If the 6 is replaced by 56, what is the new mean?
cards.body:
14

The sum rises by 50, from 20 to 70, so the mean becomes $\frac{70}{5} = 14$, while the median stays 4.

Key idea: one extreme value pulled the mean far from all the typical values. The mean is **not resistant**.

cards.title: A data set has mean 52 and median 60. In which direction is it most likely skewed?
cards.body:
Left (negatively skewed)

A long tail of low values pulls the mean below the median.

Watch out: this is a rule of thumb, not a theorem. It can fail, especially for discrete data, so confirm with a graph.
cards.searchQuery: skew direction from mean and median

cards.title: What is the 10% trimmed mean of 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 100?
cards.body:
6.5

Drop the lowest 10% and highest 10% of the sorted data (one value at each end here), then average the rest: $\frac{3 + 4 + \cdots + 10}{8} = \frac{52}{8} = 6.5$.

Why: a **trimmed mean** resists outliers yet uses most of the data. The ordinary mean here is $15.3$.

cards.title: Two groups have medians 40 and 60. Can you find the median of the combined data from these numbers and the group sizes alone?
cards.body:
No

The combined median depends on how the values are arranged within each group, not just on the two medians.

Tip: means are different. The combined mean follows from the group means and sizes: $\dfrac{n_1\bar{x}_1 + n_2\bar{x}_2}{n_1 + n_2}$.

cards.title: What is the range of the data 4, 9, 1, 15, 7?
cards.body:
14

$\text{range} = \max - \min = 15 - 1 = 14$

Watch out: it depends only on the two most extreme values, so one outlier can inflate it, and it tends to grow as more data are collected.
cards.searchQuery: range of data set max minus min

cards.title: Taking $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ as the medians of the lower and upper halves, what is the IQR of 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15?
cards.body:
6.5

The lower half $2, 4, 5, 7$ gives $Q_1 = \frac{4 + 5}{2} = 4.5$; the upper half $8, 10, 12, 15$ gives $Q_3 = \frac{10 + 12}{2} = 11$. So $\text{IQR} = 11 - 4.5 = 6.5$.

Watch out: software often interpolates quartiles, so its answer may differ slightly.
cards.searchQuery: interquartile range by hand medians of halves

cards.title: In a boxplot, what does the length of the box represent?
cards.body:
The interquartile range, $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$

The box spans the **middle 50%** of the data. A longer box means more spread in the middle half; the whiskers show the spread of the outer quarters.

cards.title: About what percent of a data set lies between $Q_1$ and the maximum?
cards.body:
About $75\%$

The four sections of a boxplot (minimum to $Q_1$, $Q_1$ to median, median to $Q_3$, $Q_3$ to maximum) each hold about 25% of the data, however long they're drawn.

Watch out: a long section means the values are **spread out**, not that there are more of them.
cards.searchQuery: percent of data between Q1 and maximum

cards.title: In a horizontal boxplot, the median sits close to $Q_1$ and the right whisker is much longer than the left. What shape is the distribution?
cards.body:
Skewed right

The upper half of the data is spread over a much wider range than the lower half, the signature of a long right tail.

Tip: a symmetric distribution shows a centered median and whiskers of similar length.

cards.title: What features of a distribution can a boxplot hide that a histogram would reveal?
cards.body:
Peaks (modes), clusters and gaps

A bimodal and a unimodal distribution can have identical five-number summaries, so their boxplots look the same.

Tip: check a **histogram** or dotplot before trusting a boxplot's picture of shape.

cards.title: When computing the variance $\sigma^2$ of an entire population of $N$ values, what do you divide the sum of squared deviations by?
cards.body:
$N$

$\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}$

Why: no correction is needed because $\mu$ is the true mean, not an estimate.
Watch out: the $n - 1$ divisor is for the **sample** variance $s^2$, which estimates $\sigma^2$ from a sample.

cards.title: Treating 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 as an entire population, what is its standard deviation $\sigma$?
cards.body:
2

$\mu = \frac{40}{8} = 5$. The squared deviations $9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16$ sum to $32$, so $\sigma^2 = \frac{32}{8} = 4$ and $\sigma = 2$.

Watch out: treated as a sample, the same data give $s = \sqrt{32/7} \approx 2.14$.

cards.title: What is the sample variance $s^2$ of the data 1, 2, 3, 4, 10?
cards.body:
12.5

$\bar{x} = 4$. The squared deviations $9, 4, 1, 0, 36$ sum to $50$, so $s^2 = \frac{50}{5 - 1} = 12.5$, in squared units.

Tip: the SD is $s = \sqrt{12.5} \approx 3.54$.

cards.title: A sample has $n = 5$, $\sum x = 20$ and $\sum x^2 = 100$. What is $s^2$?
cards.body:
5

$s^2 = \dfrac{\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2/n}{n - 1} = \dfrac{100 - 400/5}{4} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5$

It matches the deviation formula.

Watch out: on a computer the shortcut can lose precision when values are large.
cards.searchQuery: sample variance shortcut formula sum of squares

cards.title: When is the standard deviation of a data set equal to 0?
cards.body:
Only when every value is the same

The SD is the square root of an average of squared deviations, so it is never negative, and it is 0 only when every deviation is 0.

Key idea: any variation at all makes the SD positive.

cards.title: A new value exactly equal to the current mean is added to a data set. What happens to the mean and to the standard deviation?
cards.body:
The mean stays the same; the SD decreases (unless it was already 0).

The new point adds nothing to $\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2$ but raises the count, so $s^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$ gets a larger denominator with the same numerator.
cards.searchQuery: adding a value equal to the mean effect on SD

cards.title: What is the mean absolute deviation (about the mean) of 2, 4, 6, 8?
cards.body:
2

$\bar{x} = 5$, the absolute deviations are $3, 1, 1, 3$, and their average is $\frac{8}{4} = 2$.

Watch out: the **MAD** is easy to interpret but harder to work with algebraically than the SD (here $s \approx 2.58$).

cards.title: A sample has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. What is its coefficient of variation, as a percent?
cards.body:
$10\%$

$\text{CV} = \dfrac{s}{\bar{x}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{5}{50} \times 100\% = 10\%$

Why: it has no units, so the **CV** can compare variability across different scales.
Watch out: it's meaningful only for ratio-scale data with a positive mean.

cards.title: Every value in a data set with a positive mean is increased by 10. What happens to the coefficient of variation?
cards.body:
It decreases

The SD stays the same while the mean grows by 10, so $\text{CV} = \frac{s}{\bar{x}}$ shrinks.

Tip: multiplying every value by a positive constant (a change of units, for example) leaves the CV unchanged.
cards.searchQuery: coefficient of variation after adding constant

cards.title: A score is at the 80th percentile. What does that mean?
cards.body:
About $80\%$ of the scores are at or below it.

A **percentile** describes position relative to other scores.

Watch out: it is not the percent of questions answered correctly. On a hard exam, a raw score of 62% might be at the 80th percentile.

cards.title: In a class of 25, exactly 20 students scored below Ana. Defined as the percent of scores below hers, what is Ana's percentile rank?
cards.body:
80th

$\frac{20}{25} = 0.80$, so 80% scored below her.

Watch out: some textbooks count ties as half or use "at or below", which can shift a percentile rank slightly, so state the definition you use.

cards.title: The third quartile $Q_3$ is which percentile?
cards.body:
The 75th

$Q_1$, the median and $Q_3$ are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles, cutting the sorted data into four parts with about 25% of the values each.

cards.title: IQ scores have mean 100 and SD 15. What is the z-score of an IQ of 130?
cards.body:
2

$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \dfrac{130 - 100}{15} = 2$: the score is 2 standard deviations above the mean.

Why: a z-score has no units, so it can compare values measured on different scales.

cards.title: In a roughly normal distribution, a value with $z = 1$ is at about which percentile?
cards.body:
The 84th

Half the data lie below the mean, and the empirical rule puts about 34% (half of 68%) between $z = 0$ and $z = 1$: $50\% + 34\% = 84\%$.

Tip: likewise $z = -1$ is near the 16th percentile.

cards.title: A data set has $Q_1 = 40$ and $Q_3 = 60$. Is a value of 5 an outlier by the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule?
cards.body:
Yes

$\text{IQR} = 20$, so the lower fence is $40 - 1.5(20) = 10$, and $5 < 10$. (The upper fence is $60 + 30 = 90$.)

Watch out: a flagged point deserves a closer look. Don't delete it just because it's unusual.

cards.title: You find an outlier in your data. What should you do before deciding whether to remove it?
cards.body:
Investigate it: is it a recording or measurement error, or a genuine but unusual case?

Correct or remove errors, and say so. Keep genuine values.

Tip: if a genuine outlier matters, report results with and without it, or use resistant summaries such as the median and IQR.

cards.title: Weights are roughly normal with mean $50\,\mathrm{kg}$ and SD $5\,\mathrm{kg}$. By the empirical rule, about what percent weigh between $40$ and $55\,\mathrm{kg}$?
cards.body:
About $81.5\%$

$40\,\mathrm{kg}$ is 2 SD below the mean and $55\,\mathrm{kg}$ is 1 SD above.

Why: half of 95% ($47.5\%$) lies between $z = -2$ and $z = 0$, and half of 68% ($34\%$) between $z = 0$ and $z = 1$. So $47.5\% + 34\% = 81.5\%$.
cards.searchQuery: empirical rule percent between 2 SD below and 1 SD above

cards.title: By the empirical rule, about what percent of a normal distribution lies more than 3 SD below the mean?
cards.body:
About $0.15\%$

$99.7\%$ lies within 3 SD, leaving $0.3\%$ in the two tails, or $\frac{0.3\%}{2} = 0.15\%$ in each.

Tip: a value that far out is rare enough to suspect an error, or a distribution that isn't normal.
cards.searchQuery: empirical rule percent beyond 3 SD below mean

cards.title: Waiting times have mean $4\,\mathrm{min}$ and SD $5\,\mathrm{min}$. Why can't their distribution be roughly normal?
cards.body:
A normal shape would put about 16% of the times more than 1 SD below the mean, that is, below $-1\,\mathrm{min}$, which is impossible.

Key idea: when a variable can't be negative and its SD is large compared with its mean, the distribution must be **skewed right**.
cards.searchQuery: why waiting times cannot be normal mean less than SD

cards.title: By Chebyshev's inequality, at least what fraction of any data set lies within $k$ standard deviations of the mean ($k > 1$)?
cards.body:
$1 - \dfrac{1}{k^2}$

It holds for **every** distribution, whatever its shape: at least $75\%$ within 2 SD and at least $\frac{8}{9} \approx 88.9\%$ within 3 SD.

Tip: for normal data the true figures ($95\%$ and $99.7\%$) are much higher.
cards.searchQuery: Chebyshev's inequality fraction within k standard deviations

cards.title: A data set of unknown shape has mean 100 and SD 10. At least what percent of its values must lie between 80 and 120?
cards.body:
$75\%$

80 to 120 is $k = 2$ SDs on each side of the mean, and Chebyshev guarantees at least $1 - \frac{1}{2^2} = \frac{3}{4}$ of the data there.

Watch out: the empirical rule's 95% would require roughly **normal** data.

cards.title: Test scores have mean 60. Each score is multiplied by 1.5 and then 10 points are added. What is the new mean?
cards.body:
100

Measures of center follow the same transformation as the data: $1.5(60) + 10 = 100$.

Tip: the median and quartiles transform the same way, while measures of spread are only multiplied by $1.5$.
cards.searchQuery: mean after multiplying and adding constant

cards.title: A data set has IQR 12. Every value is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added. What is the new IQR?
cards.body:
36

The quartiles become $3Q_1 + 5$ and $3Q_3 + 5$, so the IQR becomes $3 \times 12 = 36$.

Why: adding a constant shifts every value equally and cancels in the difference.

cards.title: Lengths have variance $4\,\mathrm{m}^2$. After converting every length to centimeters, what is the variance in $\mathrm{cm}^2$?
cards.body:
$40{,}000\,\mathrm{cm}^2$

Multiplying data by $b$ multiplies the SD by $|b|$ and the variance by $b^2$: $100^2 \times 4 = 40{,}000$.

Tip: check with the SD. $2\,\mathrm{m} = 200\,\mathrm{cm}$, and $200^2 = 40{,}000$.
cards.searchQuery: variance after unit conversion meters to centimeters

cards.title: A data set has standard deviation 3. What is the standard deviation of $y = 10 - 2x$?
cards.body:
6

For $y = a + bx$, $s_y = |b|\,s_x = |-2| \times 3 = 6$.

Watch out: a standard deviation is never negative. The minus sign reverses the order of the data (and flips the sign of each z-score) but doesn't change the spread.

cards.title: Does converting heights from inches to centimeters change anyone's z-score?
cards.body:
No

The conversion $y = 2.54x$ multiplies each height, the mean and the SD by 2.54, which cancels in $z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}$.

Key idea: any change $y = a + bx$ with $b > 0$ leaves z-scores unchanged; with $b < 0$ they flip sign.

cards.title: In a two-way table, what is a marginal distribution?
cards.body:
The distribution of **one variable alone**, read from the row or column totals in the table's margins.

Example: in a table of class year by major, the column totals give the distribution of major for all students, ignoring year.

cards.title: In a two-way table, what is a conditional distribution?
cards.body:
The distribution of one variable among **only the individuals** with a given value of the other: percents within a single row or column.

Key idea: if the conditional distributions of one variable differ across the categories of the other, the two variables are **associated**.

cards.title: Of 200 students, 80 are seniors, and 60 of the seniors drive to school. What percent of seniors drive?
cards.body:
75%

Condition on seniors, so divide by the senior total: $\frac{60}{80} = 0.75$.

Watch out: $\frac{60}{200} = 30\%$ is the share of all students who are senior drivers (a **joint** percent), which answers a different question.
cards.searchQuery: conditional percent two-way table seniors drive

cards.title: What is Simpson's paradox?
cards.body:
A trend that holds within every group **reverses** (or disappears) when the groups are combined.

It happens when a lurking variable is unevenly spread across the groups.

Example: a treatment with higher success rates for both mild and severe cases can look worse overall if it was given mostly to severe cases.

cards.title: Hospital A saves 18 of 20 mild and 48 of 80 severe cases; Hospital B saves 64 of 80 mild and 10 of 20 severe cases. Which has the higher overall survival rate?
cards.body:
Hospital B, $74\%$ vs. $66\%$

A does better within each group ($90\%$ vs. $80\%$ for mild, $60\%$ vs. $50\%$ for severe), but most of its patients are severe cases, which drags its overall rate down: $\frac{66}{100}$ vs. $\frac{74}{100}$.

Key idea: compare within groups. This is **Simpson's paradox**.

cards.title: Which single value $c$ minimizes the sum of squared deviations $\sum (x_i - c)^2$?
cards.body:
The mean, $c = \bar{x}$

Setting the derivative $-2\sum (x_i - c)$ equal to 0 gives $c = \bar{x}$.

Why: that's why the mean pairs naturally with the variance and SD, which are built from squared deviations.
cards.searchQuery: value minimizing sum of squared deviations is the mean

cards.title: Which single value $c$ minimizes the sum of absolute deviations $\sum |x_i - c|$?
cards.body:
The median

Moving $c$ toward the side with more data points lowers the total distance, so the minimum comes where half the points lie on each side.

Tip: with an even count, any value between the two middle values works.
cards.searchQuery: value minimizing sum of absolute deviations is the median

cards.title: An investment grows by a factor of 2 one year and a factor of 8 the next. What constant yearly growth factor gives the same total growth?
cards.body:
$4$, the **geometric mean**

$\sqrt{2 \times 8} = \sqrt{16} = 4$, and indeed $4 \times 4 = 16 = 2 \times 8$.

Watch out: the arithmetic mean, $5$, would overstate the growth ($5^2 = 25$). Average growth factors with the geometric mean.

cards.title: You drive $60\,\mathrm{km}$ at $60\,\mathrm{km/h}$ and return the same $60\,\mathrm{km}$ at $40\,\mathrm{km/h}$. What is your average speed for the round trip, in $\mathrm{km/h}$?
cards.body:
$48\,\mathrm{km/h}$

Total distance over total time: $\dfrac{120\,\mathrm{km}}{1\,\mathrm{h} + 1.5\,\mathrm{h}} = 48\,\mathrm{km/h}$, the **harmonic mean** $\dfrac{2}{1/60 + 1/40}$.

Watch out: averaging the speeds gives $50$, but you spend more time at the slower speed.
cards.searchQuery: harmonic mean average speed round trip

cards.title: The sample variance $s^2$ is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$. Is the sample SD $s$ an unbiased estimator of $\sigma$?
cards.body:
No: on average, $s$ slightly underestimates $\sigma$.

The square root is concave, so $E(s) = E\left(\sqrt{s^2}\right) < \sqrt{E(s^2)} = \sigma$ whenever $s$ varies from sample to sample (Jensen's inequality).

Tip: the bias shrinks as $n$ grows and is usually ignored in practice.
cards.searchQuery: sample standard deviation biased estimator of sigma

cards.title: Each of $n$ values is standardized using the sample mean and sample SD $s$. What is the sum of the squared z-scores?
cards.body:
$n - 1$

$\sum z_i^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{s^2}$, and $s^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$, so the ratio is exactly $n - 1$.

Watch out: standardizing with the divide-by-$n$ SD would give $n$.
cards.searchQuery: sum of squared z-scores equals n minus 1

cards.title: For normally distributed data, the IQR is about how many standard deviations wide?
cards.body:
About $1.35$

The quartiles of a normal distribution sit at $z \approx \pm 0.674$, so $\text{IQR} \approx 1.349\sigma$.

Tip: turned around, $\text{IQR}/1.35$ gives a resistant estimate of $\sigma$.
cards.searchQuery: IQR of normal distribution 1.35 standard deviations

cards.title: For perfectly normal data, about what percent of values fall outside the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ fences?
cards.body:
About $0.7\%$

The upper fence sits at $Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR} \approx 0.674\sigma + 1.5(1.349\sigma) \approx 2.70\sigma$ above the mean (the lower fence mirrors it), and only about $0.7\%$ of a normal distribution lies beyond $\pm 2.70\sigma$.

Key idea: large normal samples still show a few flagged points.
cards.searchQuery: percent of normal data flagged as outliers by IQR rule
